History and Physical (Detailed)

Consult Summary:
30-year-old man with 3-day history of loose stools (4–5×/day) with mild abdominal pain and one episode of vomiting, clinically consistent with an acute self-limiting gastroenteritis; counselled on hydration, soft diet, red-flag monitoring, and over-the-counter oral rehydration salts.

History:
• Presenting complaint: “Bad diarrhoea” for 3 days.  
• Timeline/character:
  – Day 0: Sudden onset of loose/watery stools.  
  – Currently 4–5 bowel motions per day, variable consistency.  
  – Mild lower abdominal pain.  
  – One isolated vomiting episode.  
  – Possible low-grade fever (patient unsure).  
  – ↓ appetite but able to maintain oral intake of fluids.  
• No blood or mucus in stool.  
• No recent travel, suspicious food, or antibiotic use.  
• No medications taken yet for diarrhoea or pain.  

Past Medical History:
• Asthma – uses an inhaler called “Lexapro” (possible naming error; details unclear).  
• No other chronic illnesses reported.

Medications:
• “Lexapro” inhaler – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• No over-the-counter or prescription medicines for current episode.  
Allergies:
• Denies drug, food, or environmental allergies.

Social History:
• Social habits (smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs) not discussed.  
• Occupation and living circumstances not discussed.

Family History:
• Father: Hypertension; died of bowel cancer at age 62.  
• No other familial illnesses reported.

Physical Examination:
• General: Clinician notes patient “doesn’t look dehydrated.”  
• Vitals: Not recorded.  
• System examinations: Not recorded.

Investigations:
• None performed or ordered at this visit.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Acute infectious gastroenteritis (most likely viral) causing mild, self-limited watery diarrhoea.

DDx Integration (concise):
1. Acute viral gastroenteritis – fits short course, watery stools, mild systemic symptoms.  
2. Acute bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis – possible but no high-risk food/travel; no blood.  
3. Medication-related diarrhoea (escitalopram if truly taken) – less likely; symptoms abrupt after chronic use (opposing evidence).

Issue 1 – Acute diarrhoea:
Assessment:
• Likely viral gastroenteritis; no alarm features (blood, severe pain, high fever, dehydration).  
Plan:
• Oral rehydration: Encourage ≥2 L water/day plus OTC Dioralyte per packet instructions.  
• Diet: 48 h soft/bland foods (toast, crackers, mashed vegetables); avoid dairy, meat, fish, eggs initially; yogurt/probiotics allowed.  
• Symptom control: May use simple analgesia (e.g., acetaminophen) if needed – none prescribed today.  
• Red-flags/return: Seek care if ≥6–8 watery stools/day, signs of dehydration, blood or mucus in stool, persistent fever, or duration >1 week.  
• If diarrhoea persists or blood appears → arrange stool culture ± antibiotics.  
• Documentation: Advice recorded in app for patient review.

Issue 2 – Asthma:
Assessment:
• Stable; uses “Lexapro” inhaler (name unclear).  
Plan:
• Verify correct inhaler and technique at next routine review.  
• No changes today.

Issue 3 – Family history of bowel cancer:
Assessment:
• Father diagnosed at 62 y; patient age 40 (born 09/29/1983).  
Plan:
• Discuss colorectal cancer screening at next physical; not urgent in today’s acute visit.

General:
• Provide written information on acute diarrhoea management.  
• Follow-up virtual consult PRN or sooner if red-flags emerge.

Quality checks:
• Missing expected data: vitals, full systems review, smoking/alcohol history, detailed medication list, inhaler verification.  
• Transcript/medication name ambiguity: “Lexapro” described as yellow inhaler (conflict with SSRI tablet); noted but unresolved.  
• Overall transcript clear; occasional inaudible words did not affect clinical content.
